name: Entrepreneurship Fundamentals
description: An action-oriented introduction to entrepreneurship — idea generation, problem-solving, lean startup methodology, business model design, pitching, and building an entrepreneurial mindset.

modules.title: The Entrepreneurial Mindset
modules.objectives: Cultivate a growth mindset; understand failure as a learning tool; develop creativity and resilience. Students will analyze examples, explain how an entrepreneurial mindset changes a response to failure, and create a short written or visual product that demonstrates personal application.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Entrepreneurship §1.3, “The Entrepreneurial Mindset” — read the section on productive habits, failure, and persistence.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.video2Note: Y Combinator — Lecture 1: How to Start a Startup (Sam Altman and Dustin Moskovitz); title verified by YouTube oEmbed on 2026-09-07.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 1 Review — answer question 11 on the entrepreneurial mindset, then complete the GIIS reflection assignment.
modules.assignment: Write a 1-page personal reflection: describe a time you failed at something and what you learned from it. Then list 3 qualities you want to strengthen as an entrepreneur and explain how you plan to develop them. Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. Include: notes, examples, evidence, calculations, sources, or analysis from the The Entrepreneurial Mindset module, plus a short explanation of how your work supports your answer. Evaluation: the teacher should be able to see the final product, the steps or evidence used, and one clear connection to the module objective.

modules.title: Identifying Problems & Opportunities
modules.objectives: Apply design thinking principles; create an empathy map; identify customer pain points; recognize gaps in the market. Students will analyze a real observation, create an empathy map with evidence, distinguish pain points from proposed solutions, and justify one testable opportunity.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Entrepreneurship §6.3, “Design Thinking” — read the human-centered observation, ideation, prototyping, and testing process.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 6 Review — answer questions 9–12 on design thinking and observation, then complete the GIIS empathy-map assignment.
modules.assignment: Choose a problem you observe in your school or community. Create an empathy map for the people affected using at least three specific anonymized observations. List at least 5 pain points and 2 potential market gaps. Mark each pain point as an observed problem rather than a proposed solution. Choose the strongest gap and write one testable opportunity statement, citing the observation that supports it. Submit: the empathy map, observations, pain-point list, market gaps, and opportunity statement. Include: three anonymized observations, evidence beside each pain point, and one sentence separating the opportunity from any proposed solution. Evaluation: the teacher will check evidence quality, problem-versus-solution accuracy, empathy-map completeness, and whether the opportunity is testable and justified.

modules.title: Ideation Techniques
modules.objectives: Apply brainstorming, SCAMPER, mind mapping, and lateral thinking to generate creative business ideas. Students will define a target customer and success criterion, generate alternatives with two ideation methods, and evaluate which idea best fits the identified need.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Entrepreneurship §6.2, “Creative Problem-Solving Process” — read the creativity and brainstorming process before applying SCAMPER and mind mapping in GIIS.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.video2Note: TED — How to build your creative confidence (David Kelley); title verified by YouTube oEmbed on 2026-09-07.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 6 Review — answer questions 5–8 on creativity, brainstorming, teams, and storyboarding, then complete the GIIS ideation assignment.
modules.assignment: Define the target customer and one success criterion for an idea that addresses the Module 2 opportunity. Run a timed 10-minute brainstorm, apply SCAMPER to your top idea, and create a mind map connecting your best 5 ideas to customer needs. Compare the five ideas in a small decision matrix using customer fit, feasibility, and the stated success criterion; choose one and justify the choice. Submit: the brainstorm, SCAMPER notes, mind map, decision matrix, and choice explanation. Include: a named target customer, the pre-set success criterion, all five alternatives, matrix ratings, and evidence for the final choice. Evaluation: the teacher will check use of two ideation methods, variety of alternatives, explicit criteria, and evidence-based selection.

modules.title: Customer Discovery
modules.objectives: Design and conduct customer interviews; validate assumptions; apply the jobs-to-be-done framework to understand customer motivations. Students will design neutral interview questions, document responses without private contact data, compare findings with initial assumptions, and revise one jobs-to-be-done statement.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Entrepreneurship §8.2, “Market Research, Market Opportunity Recognition, and Target Market” — focus on primary research and evidence about target customers; use the GIIS lesson for neutral interviews and jobs-to-be-done.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 8 Review — answer questions 6–7 on market research and primary versus secondary data, then complete the GIIS customer-interview assignment.
modules.assignment: Write 10 open-ended customer-interview questions and interview at least two people; self-paced learners may use family members, friends, teachers, or peers who reasonably fit the target-user profile. Submit: the questions, anonymized response notes, a findings summary, and one jobs-to-be-done statement. Include: which assumptions were supported or challenged, what surprised you, and one product or research decision revised because of the evidence; do not include private contact information. Evaluation: the teacher will check neutral questions, accurate notes, clear comparison with initial assumptions, and a decision justified by the interview evidence.

modules.title: The Lean Startup
modules.objectives: Understand the build-measure-learn cycle; define and build a minimum viable product (MVP); understand when and how to pivot. Students will identify a risky assumption, design an MVP to test it, define a behavioral success metric, and explain whether the evidence supports a pivot or another test.
modules.readingNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.videoNote: The Swedish Investor — The Lean Startup Summary (by Eric Ries); title verified by YouTube oEmbed on 2026-09-07.
modules.video2Note: Interloper Films — Eric Ries explains The Pivot; title verified by YouTube oEmbed on 2026-09-07.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Design and run a small, safe MVP test for your business idea. State: (1) the single risky assumption, (2) the simplest product or service that tests it, (3) one behavioral success threshold set before the test, and (4) a no-cost or low-risk test with at least two suitable target users; collect only anonymized, non-sensitive outcomes and do not accept payments. Submit: the one-page MVP design, test protocol, outcome table, and a short build-measure-learn decision explaining whether the evidence supports persevering, revising the test, or pivoting. Include: the pre-set threshold, dates or sequence of the test, anonymized results for each participant, and a decision tied directly to the results. Evaluation: the teacher will check assumption-to-MVP fit, pre-set metric, accurate outcome evidence, privacy/safety, and a decision justified by the result.

modules.title: Business Model Canvas
modules.objectives: Identify and explain all nine building blocks of the Business Model Canvas; articulate a clear value proposition, customer segments, and revenue streams.
modules.readingNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.videoNote: Strategyzer — Business Model Canvas Explained; title verified by YouTube oEmbed on 2026-09-07.
modules.video2Note: Strategyzer — Visualizing Your Business Model; title verified by YouTube oEmbed on 2026-09-07.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Complete a full Business Model Canvas for your startup idea. Fill in all nine blocks with specific, concrete details (not generic descriptions). Write a 1-paragraph summary explaining how your value proposition connects to your customer segment and revenue streams. Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. Include: notes, examples, evidence, calculations, sources, or analysis from the Business Model Canvas module, plus a short explanation of how your work supports your answer. Evaluation: the teacher should be able to see the final product, the steps or evidence used, and one clear connection to the module objective.

modules.title: Market Research & Competitive Analysis
modules.objectives: Distinguish primary from secondary research; map the competitive landscape; identify your differentiation strategy. Students will collect primary and secondary evidence, compare direct and indirect competitors across customer-relevant criteria, and justify one defensible differentiation claim.
modules.readingNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Use at least one primary source (such as anonymized Module 4 interview evidence) and two credible secondary sources to identify at least 2 direct competitors and 1 indirect alternative; add up to 2 more only when genuine alternatives exist. Create a competitive matrix using 4 customer-relevant criteria, cite the source for every factual comparison, and label each source as primary or secondary. Write a paragraph that makes one defensible differentiation claim and explains how the evidence supports it. Submit: source notes, citations or links, the matrix, and the differentiation paragraph. Include: at least one primary and two secondary sources, source labels, links or citations for factual claims, and the criteria used in the matrix. Evaluation: the teacher will check source classification, evidence traceability, direct-versus-indirect accuracy, fair comparison, and whether the claim follows from the evidence; a justified three-competitor matrix can earn full credit.

modules.title: Value Proposition Design
modules.objectives: Craft a compelling value proposition; define your unique selling point (USP); position and pitch your product clearly. Students will identify a target customer, define a measurable or observable benefit, create three value-proposition versions, revise the strongest one using recorded feedback, and present it in a concise pitch.
modules.readingNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Write three one-sentence value propositions: one focused on the customer problem, one on the solution’s benefit, and one on differentiation. Ask a peer, family member, or advisor to explain what each version promises and which is clearest. Submit: the three drafts, an anonymized feedback summary, the revised final value proposition, a brief choice explanation, and a 60-second written, audio, or video pitch. Include: a target customer, a measurable or observable benefit with its indicator, a credible reason to choose the solution, one revision tied to the feedback, and a pitch that states the problem, solution, benefit, and next step. Evaluation: the teacher will check clarity, customer relevance, benefit measurability, specificity, differentiation, evidence that feedback improved the final version, and whether the pitch communicates the value proposition accurately within 60 seconds.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a growth mindset in entrepreneurship?
options: Believing your abilities are fixed and cannot change
Viewing failure as a permanent setback
Seeing challenges as opportunities to learn and improve
Avoiding risks to preserve existing success
questions.answer: Seeing challenges as opportunities to learn and improve
questions.explanation: A growth mindset means believing abilities can be developed through dedication and hard work, treating failures as learning experiences rather than permanent defeats.

questions.question: The first step in design thinking, as used in opportunity identification, is:
options: Prototyping
Testing
Empathizing
Defining
questions.answer: Empathizing
questions.explanation: Design thinking begins with empathizing — deeply understanding the people you are designing for and the problems they face before defining or solving anything.

questions.question: SCAMPER is a technique used during which phase of the entrepreneurial process?
options: Customer discovery
Ideation
Financial modeling
Legal formation
questions.answer: Ideation
questions.explanation: SCAMPER (Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to other uses, Eliminate, Reverse) is an ideation technique used to generate creative ideas by modifying existing concepts.

questions.question: In customer discovery, what is the primary purpose of interviewing potential customers?
options: Test assumptions about their needs and current behavior
Pitch the product until the interviewee agrees to buy it
Ask leading questions that confirm the founder's preferred solution
Collect only demographic facts without discussing the problem
questions.answer: Test assumptions about their needs and current behavior
questions.explanation: Customer discovery uses neutral questions about real experiences and behavior to test assumptions. Pitching or leading the interview biases the evidence, and demographics alone do not reveal the customer's problem.

questions.question: What does MVP stand for in the lean startup methodology?
options: Most Valuable Product
Minimum Viable Product
Maximum Value Proposition
Market Validation Process
questions.answer: Minimum Viable Product
questions.explanation: An MVP (Minimum Viable Product) is the simplest version of a product that allows a team to collect validated learning about customers with the least effort.

questions.question: In the lean startup build-measure-learn cycle, what happens immediately after you BUILD your MVP?
options: You pivot your business model
You measure the results of your experiment
You raise funding
You hire a team
questions.answer: You measure the results of your experiment
questions.explanation: The build-measure-learn loop requires measuring customer response data after building the MVP before deciding to persevere or pivot.

questions.question: The Business Model Canvas contains how many building blocks?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: 9.

questions.question: Which activity is primary market research?
options: Running a focus group with prospective users
Reading an industry report from a research firm
Comparing statistics in a government database
Reviewing competitors' published price pages
questions.answer: Running a focus group with prospective users
questions.explanation: A focus group gathers new data directly from potential customers, so it is primary research. Reports, databases, and published competitor information are existing secondary sources.

questions.question: A competitive advantage describes:
options: How much money a startup has raised
The unique attribute that allows a business to outperform competitors
The number of employees a company has
The speed at which a company launches its product
questions.answer: The unique attribute that allows a business to outperform competitors
questions.explanation: A competitive advantage is the distinct quality (lower cost, unique feature, stronger brand, etc.) that allows a business to generate more value for customers than its rivals.

questions.question: The 'jobs-to-be-done' framework focuses on:
options: The technical specifications of a product
The underlying task or goal a customer is trying to accomplish
The number of job openings at a startup
The legal requirements for hiring employees
questions.answer: The underlying task or goal a customer is trying to accomplish
questions.explanation: Jobs-to-be-done theory argues that customers 'hire' products to help them make progress in their lives — focusing on what job they need done rather than demographics.

questions.question: Which building block of the Business Model Canvas describes the group of people or organizations a business aims to reach?
options: Value Proposition
Revenue Streams
Customer Segments
Key Activities
questions.answer: Customer Segments
questions.explanation: Customer Segments defines the different groups of people or organizations an enterprise aims to reach and serve.

questions.question: In lean startup practice, what does it mean to pivot?
options: Change a fundamental part of the strategy in response to validated learning
Continue the original plan without changes despite contrary evidence
Move the company's office to a different location
Add features without identifying which assumption they test
questions.answer: Change a fundamental part of the strategy in response to validated learning
questions.explanation: A pivot is a deliberate strategic change grounded in evidence while keeping a broader vision. Persisting ignores contrary evidence, and changing a location or adding untested features is not automatically a pivot.

questions.question: An empathy map typically captures which four dimensions of a user's experience?
options: Price, Product, Place, Promotion
Say, Think, Do, Feel
Problem, Solution, Market, Revenue
Customers, Channels, Costs, Competition
questions.answer: Say, Think, Do, Feel
questions.explanation: An empathy map captures what users Say, Think, Do, and Feel — helping teams build deeper empathy and gain insight into customer needs.

questions.question: Describe the difference between primary and secondary market research. Give one example of each and explain when you would use each type for a startup.
questions.answer: Primary research collects new, original data directly (e.g., customer interviews, surveys). Secondary research uses existing published data (e.g., industry reports, census data). Primary research is best when you need specific insights about your target customer's exact problems; secondary research is useful for understanding market size or broader trends without the cost of original data collection.
questions.explanation: Both types are complementary: secondary research helps frame the landscape; primary research validates specific assumptions about your customer.

questions.question: Explain the build-measure-learn cycle in your own words. Why is it important for a startup to go through this loop quickly?
questions.answer: Build-measure-learn: build the smallest possible version of your product (MVP), measure how real customers respond, and learn whether your assumptions were correct. Speed is critical because early-stage startups have limited resources; the faster they run experiments, the sooner they can validate or invalidate ideas before spending money on the wrong direction.
questions.explanation: The loop reduces waste by testing assumptions cheaply and quickly, enabling data-driven decisions rather than guesswork.

questions.question: Choose the best answer: Resilience in entrepreneurship is best described as:
options: Recovering from setbacks, learning, and continuing to improve
Never making mistakes
Abilities can be developed through effort and learning
Seeing challenges as opportunities to learn and improve
questions.answer: Recovering from setbacks, learning, and continuing to improve
questions.explanation: The best answer is Recovering from setbacks, learning, and continuing to improve.

questions.question: Which design thinking phase involves generating as many ideas as possible without judgment?
options: Empathize
Define
Ideate
Test
questions.answer: Ideate
questions.explanation: The Ideate phase encourages divergent thinking — generating a large volume of ideas freely before narrowing down to the best solutions.

questions.question: A startup's value proposition answers which core question?
options: How much does the product cost?
Why should a customer choose you over the alternatives?
How many employees do you have?
When will the product launch?
questions.answer: Why should a customer choose you over the alternatives?
questions.explanation: A value proposition communicates the specific benefits a product delivers and why those benefits make it the best choice for the target customer compared to alternatives.

questions.question: Which interview question is most useful for unbiased customer discovery?
options: Would you buy my amazing study app?
Tell me about the last time you struggled to find study help.
Do you agree that students need my solution?
How much do you like this logo?
questions.answer: Tell me about the last time you struggled to find study help.
questions.explanation: A neutral question about a recent real experience produces stronger evidence than pitching or asking for agreement.

questions.question: Which statement describes a customer pain point rather than a proposed solution?
options: Students wait several days to receive feedback on practice work.
Build an AI feedback app.
Add a chatbot to the website.
Sell a premium subscription.
questions.answer: Students wait several days to receive feedback on practice work.
questions.explanation: A pain point describes an observed problem; the other choices propose products or business decisions.

questions.question: In SCAMPER, what does the letter C prompt an entrepreneur to do?
options: Calculate profit
Combine elements or ideas
Copy a competitor exactly
Cancel customer interviews
questions.answer: Combine elements or ideas
questions.explanation: SCAMPER uses C for Combine, a prompt for generating alternatives by joining features, processes, or ideas.

questions.question: Before building an MVP, a founder should first identify:
options: The riskiest assumption the MVP must test
Every feature the final product might include
The permanent company logo
A five-year hiring plan
questions.answer: The riskiest assumption the MVP must test
questions.explanation: An MVP is designed around a specific risky assumption so its result produces useful learning.

questions.question: After launching an MVP experiment, which result provides the strongest evidence?
options: A founder says the idea feels promising.
Target users complete the intended behavior at the pre-set success rate.
Friends say the colors look good.
The MVP includes many features.
questions.answer: Target users complete the intended behavior at the pre-set success rate.
questions.explanation: A defined behavioral metric tests the assumption more directly than opinions or feature count.

questions.question: When is a pivot justified in lean startup practice?
options: When repeated evidence contradicts a key assumption and suggests a better direction
Whenever one person dislikes the logo
Before collecting any customer evidence
Only after building the full product
questions.answer: When repeated evidence contradicts a key assumption and suggests a better direction
questions.explanation: A pivot is an evidence-based strategic change, not an impulsive reaction or a substitute for testing.

questions.question: Which Business Model Canvas block identifies the groups a startup intends to serve?
options: Customer Segments
Key Activities
Cost Structure
Key Partnerships
questions.answer: Customer Segments
questions.explanation: Customer Segments defines the distinct groups of people or organizations the business aims to reach and serve.

questions.question: Which Business Model Canvas block explains how the business earns money from each customer segment?
options: Revenue Streams
Channels
Key Resources
Customer Relationships
questions.answer: Revenue Streams
questions.explanation: Revenue Streams describes the ways customers pay and the business captures value.

questions.question: Which activity is primary market research?
options: Interviewing five target users with neutral questions
Reading a published industry report
Reviewing public competitor websites
Using census statistics
questions.answer: Interviewing five target users with neutral questions
questions.explanation: Primary research collects new evidence directly from relevant people; the other choices use existing secondary sources.

questions.question: Which is an indirect competitor for a student tutoring app?
options: Another on-demand tutoring app
A free study group organized by the school
The same app sold in another city
A tutoring app with a different color scheme
questions.answer: A free study group organized by the school
questions.explanation: An indirect competitor solves the same customer need through a different kind of offering.

questions.question: A defensible differentiation claim should be based on:
options: Customer-relevant evidence and a clear comparison with alternatives
A claim that no competitor can ever copy
The founder’s personal preference alone
The largest possible list of features
questions.answer: Customer-relevant evidence and a clear comparison with alternatives
questions.explanation: Differentiation is credible when it matters to the target customer and is supported by comparison evidence.

questions.question: The jobs-to-be-done framework focuses on:
options: The progress or task a customer is trying to accomplish
The founder’s preferred product features
The number of employees a startup needs
The legal title of each job
questions.answer: The progress or task a customer is trying to accomplish
questions.explanation: Jobs-to-be-done frames demand around the progress customers seek, rather than around a proposed solution.

questions.question: Which empathy-map evidence is strongest?
options: An exact anonymized observation of what a target user said and did
A guess about what all teenagers want
A feature list copied from a competitor
A slogan written by the founder
questions.answer: An exact anonymized observation of what a target user said and did
questions.explanation: Evidence tied to observed words and behavior is more reliable than unsupported assumptions.

questions.question: Which value proposition is most specific and testable?
options: For ninth-grade writers, weekly 15-minute feedback identifies one revision priority before the next draft.
We make education better for everyone.
Our product is innovative and high quality.
Students will love our amazing platform.
questions.answer: For ninth-grade writers, weekly 15-minute feedback identifies one revision priority before the next draft.
questions.explanation: A strong value proposition names a target customer, a concrete benefit, and a measurable or observable result.

questions.question: Name the nine Business Model Canvas blocks. Then define any three of them and explain one reasonable relationship among those three for a startup of your choice.
questions.answer: The nine blocks are Customer Segments, Value Propositions, Channels, Customer Relationships, Revenue Streams, Key Resources, Key Activities, Key Partnerships, and Cost Structure. Example for a food-delivery startup: Customer Segments are the distinct groups a venture serves; Value Propositions are the benefits offered to solve those customers’ problems; and Key Activities are the essential actions the venture must perform. Serving busy urban professionals with dependable delivery requires logistics coordination as a key activity, so the selected customer segment shapes both the promised benefit and the work needed to deliver it. Equivalent accurate definitions and reasonable relationships are acceptable.
questions.explanation: Score the 2-point item as follows: 0.5 for naming all nine blocks (award proportional partial credit for omissions), 0.75 for three accurate definitions (0.25 each), and 0.75 for a clear, reasonable relationship among the selected blocks. Accept equivalent examples; outside evidence is not required.

questions.question: You have an idea for a new student tutoring app. Outline the key steps you would take — from idea to MVP — using the lean startup approach. What would your MVP look like, and how would you measure its success?
questions.answer: A strong response: (1) identifies a core assumption; (2) proposes an appropriate customer-discovery step using a reasonable number of relevant participants, consistent with the taught assignment; (3) builds the simplest MVP that tests the assumption, such as a booking form plus manually coordinated tutoring; (4) defines a behavioral success metric; and (5) uses the result to persevere, revise, or pivot. Exact interview counts and MVP formats may vary when justified.
questions.explanation: Score the lean-startup sequence, fit between assumption and MVP, and specificity of the behavioral success measure. Do not require ten interviews or the sample MVP; accept reasonable evidence plans consistent with the module.

questions.question: For a startup offering weekly writing feedback to ninth-grade students, write two one-sentence value propositions. Choose the stronger one and explain how one piece of customer or competitor evidence would help you revise it.
questions.answer: A strong response gives two distinct, specific value propositions, selects one using a customer-relevant criterion, and names concrete evidence such as interview behavior, willingness to try, turnaround-time needs, or a competitor comparison. Example: “Ninth-grade writers receive one teacher-reviewed revision priority within 24 hours so they can improve the next draft.” Equivalent evidence-based responses are acceptable.
questions.explanation: Score specificity of target customer and benefit, meaningful comparison between versions, and a concrete evidence plan. Do not require the sample wording.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following best defines an entrepreneurial mindset?
options: Focusing only on making money quickly
Approaching problems with creativity, persistence, and a willingness to learn from failure
Avoiding any risks in business decisions
Copying successful business ideas from others
quizQuestions.answer: Approaching problems with creativity, persistence, and a willingness to learn from failure
quizQuestions.explanation: An entrepreneurial mindset involves seeing opportunities in problems, embracing calculated risk, and treating setbacks as learning experiences.

quizQuestions.question: A growth mindset, as defined by Carol Dweck, is the belief that:
options: Intelligence and talent are fixed at birth
Abilities can be developed through effort and learning
Only naturally gifted people can succeed
Success depends entirely on luck
quizQuestions.answer: Abilities can be developed through effort and learning
quizQuestions.explanation: Carol Dweck's growth mindset research shows that people who believe abilities can grow through dedication outperform those with a fixed mindset.

quizQuestions.question: After a product test fails, which response best demonstrates a growth mindset?
options: Identify what the result teaches, revise one assumption, and test again
Conclude that entrepreneurial ability is fixed and quit
Hide the result so the original idea appears successful
Repeat the identical test without examining the evidence
quizQuestions.answer: Identify what the result teaches, revise one assumption, and test again
quizQuestions.explanation: A growth mindset treats failure as evidence for learning and improvement. Hiding, repeating without reflection, or treating ability as fixed prevents learning.

quizQuestions.question: Design thinking begins with which phase?
options: Prototype
Test
Empathize
Define
quizQuestions.answer: Empathize
quizQuestions.explanation: Design thinking starts with empathizing — deeply understanding the people you are designing for to uncover their real needs.

quizQuestions.question: An empathy map helps entrepreneurs:
options: Calculate startup costs
Understand what customers think, feel, say, and do
Design a company logo
Choose a legal structure for the business
quizQuestions.answer: Understand what customers think, feel, say, and do
quizQuestions.explanation: Empathy maps are visual tools that capture insights about users across four dimensions: what they Say, Think, Do, and Feel.

quizQuestions.question: A 'pain point' in the context of identifying customer problems refers to:
options: A physical injury a customer sustains
A specific problem, frustration, or unmet need that a customer experiences
The price a customer pays for a product
A complaint about poor customer service
quizQuestions.answer: A specific problem, frustration, or unmet need that a customer experiences
quizQuestions.explanation: Pain points are the problems or challenges customers face that create opportunities for entrepreneurs to deliver solutions.

quizQuestions.question: Which empathy-map observation is a customer pain point rather than a proposed solution?
options: Students wait twenty minutes to buy lunch and often miss part of recess
Build a mobile pre-ordering application
Sell lunches at a lower price
Advertise the cafeteria on social media
quizQuestions.answer: Students wait twenty minutes to buy lunch and often miss part of recess
quizQuestions.explanation: A pain point describes the customer's current difficulty and its consequence. The other choices are proposed solutions or marketing decisions that should be evaluated only after the problem is understood.

quizQuestions.question: The SCAMPER technique uses which of the following actions to generate new ideas?
options: Survey, Compare, Analyze, Measure, Plan, Execute, Review
Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to other uses, Eliminate, Reverse
Sell, Create, Apply, Market, Price, Evaluate, Release
Start, Configure, Adjust, Manage, Promote, Evolve, Replicate
quizQuestions.answer: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to other uses, Eliminate, Reverse
quizQuestions.explanation: SCAMPER is an ideation checklist: each letter prompts a different way to transform an existing idea into something new.

quizQuestions.question: The key rule of effective brainstorming is:
options: Evaluate each idea immediately to save time
Only share ideas you are confident about
Generate as many ideas as possible without judging them during the session
Focus only on practical, low-cost ideas
quizQuestions.answer: Generate as many ideas as possible without judging them during the session
quizQuestions.explanation: Brainstorming works best when judgment is suspended — quantity over quality during idea generation encourages creative thinking.

quizQuestions.question: Lateral thinking, as a creative technique, involves:
options: Following established procedures step by step
Approaching problems from unexpected angles to find unconventional solutions
Using data to identify the most logical solution
Consulting experts for the correct answer
quizQuestions.answer: Approaching problems from unexpected angles to find unconventional solutions
quizQuestions.explanation: Lateral thinking (coined by Edward de Bono) challenges assumptions and looks for indirect, creative approaches rather than straightforward logical paths.

quizQuestions.question: The main goal of a customer discovery interview is to:
options: Convince the customer to buy your product
Understand the customer's actual problems and behaviors
Explain all the features of your product
Gather positive testimonials for marketing
quizQuestions.answer: Understand the customer's actual problems and behaviors
quizQuestions.explanation: Customer discovery is about listening and learning, not selling. You want to uncover real pain points and test your assumptions about who the customer is.

quizQuestions.question: Which type of question is most effective in a customer discovery interview?
options: 'Would you buy a product like this?'
'Don't you think this is a great idea?'
'Tell me about the last time you experienced this problem.'
'How much would you pay for this solution?'
quizQuestions.answer: 'Tell me about the last time you experienced this problem.'
quizQuestions.explanation: Open-ended behavioral questions reveal real experiences and needs; 'would you buy' questions produce unreliable hypothetical answers.

quizQuestions.question: The jobs-to-be-done (JTBD) framework focuses on:
options: The demographic profile of target customers
The functional and emotional progress a customer is trying to make in their life
The technical specifications of a product feature
The number of employment positions a startup plans to create
quizQuestions.answer: The functional and emotional progress a customer is trying to make in their life
quizQuestions.explanation: JTBD theory holds that customers 'hire' products to make progress — solve a problem or achieve a goal — rather than for product features alone.

quizQuestions.question: Validating an assumption in customer discovery means:
options: Proving that your product works technically
Confirming (or refuting) your hypothesis about a customer's problem or behavior with real evidence
Getting legal validation from a lawyer
Validating your business plan with an accountant
quizQuestions.answer: Confirming (or refuting) your hypothesis about a customer's problem or behavior with real evidence
quizQuestions.explanation: Assumption validation uses real customer data — gathered through interviews or experiments — to determine whether your beliefs about the market are accurate.

quizQuestions.question: The correct order of the lean startup cycle is:
options: Measure → Build → Learn
Learn → Build → Measure
Build → Measure → Learn
Plan → Build → Launch
quizQuestions.answer: Build → Measure → Learn
quizQuestions.explanation: The lean startup loop is: Build (create the MVP), Measure (collect data on user behavior), Learn (extract insights to decide what to do next).

quizQuestions.question: The purpose of an MVP is to:
options: Create a perfect product before launch
Test the most important assumption with the least effort
Impress investors with advanced features
Compete directly with established market leaders from day one
quizQuestions.answer: Test the most important assumption with the least effort
quizQuestions.explanation: An MVP is the smallest experiment that tests your riskiest assumption, allowing you to learn quickly without over-investing in a product that may need to change.

quizQuestions.question: Which measure would best test whether a tutoring MVP solves an urgent customer problem?
options: The percentage of trial users who book and complete a second session
The number of colors used in the landing-page design
The founder's confidence in the idea
The total number of features planned for next year
quizQuestions.answer: The percentage of trial users who book and complete a second session
quizQuestions.explanation: Repeat use is behavior tied to whether customers receive enough value to return. Design choices, founder confidence, and planned features do not measure whether the MVP solves the problem.

quizQuestions.question: A team tests an MVP and learns that customers value speed more than customization. What is the strongest next step?
options: Revise the product hypothesis toward faster delivery and run a new test
Add more customization without measuring demand
Launch nationally before testing the new insight
Ignore the result because it conflicts with the original plan
quizQuestions.answer: Revise the product hypothesis toward faster delivery and run a new test
quizQuestions.explanation: Build-measure-learn requires the team to turn evidence into a revised hypothesis and another test. Expanding, adding unsupported features, or ignoring the result increases risk without learning.

quizQuestions.question: How many building blocks does the Business Model Canvas have?
quizQuestions.explanation: The Business Model Canvas has nine building blocks covering customers, value, infrastructure, and finances.

quizQuestions.question: The 'Value Proposition' block in the Business Model Canvas describes:
options: The price of your product
The bundle of products and services that create value for a specific customer segment
The marketing channels you use to reach customers
The costs required to operate the business
quizQuestions.answer: The bundle of products and services that create value for a specific customer segment
quizQuestions.explanation: The Value Proposition is the reason customers choose you — it describes the specific value you deliver to solve their problems or fulfill their needs.

quizQuestions.question: Revenue Streams in the Business Model Canvas represent:
options: The costs the company incurs
The cash a company generates from each customer segment
The channels used to deliver the product
The key partners that support the business
quizQuestions.answer: The cash a company generates from each customer segment
quizQuestions.explanation: Revenue Streams describe how the company earns money from its value propositions — through sales, subscriptions, licensing, advertising, etc.

quizQuestions.question: Which Business Model Canvas block should list outside suppliers whose cooperation is essential to deliver the product?
options: Key Partners
Key Resources
Customer Relationships
Revenue Streams
quizQuestions.answer: Key Partners
quizQuestions.explanation: Key Partners identifies outside organizations or suppliers the business relies on. Key Resources are assets the business controls, while Customer Relationships and Revenue Streams describe customer interaction and income.

quizQuestions.question: What is the difference between primary and secondary market research?
options: Primary research is more expensive; secondary research is free
Primary research collects new data directly; secondary research uses existing data
Primary research is conducted by large companies; secondary by startups
Primary research uses quantitative methods only; secondary uses qualitative methods only
quizQuestions.answer: Primary research collects new data directly; secondary research uses existing data
quizQuestions.explanation: Primary research (surveys, interviews, experiments) generates new data for your specific question. Secondary research uses existing data (reports, studies) already published.

quizQuestions.question: A competitive analysis helps entrepreneurs:
options: Copy competitors' products exactly
Understand the competitive landscape and identify how to differentiate
Eliminate all competitors from the market
Determine the salary structure for employees
quizQuestions.answer: Understand the competitive landscape and identify how to differentiate
quizQuestions.explanation: Competitive analysis reveals who else is solving a similar problem, how they do it, and where gaps exist — informing differentiation strategy.

quizQuestions.question: A competing service does not offer same-day setup. Which statement is a testable differentiation hypothesis rather than an unsupported conclusion?
options: Our service is already the market leader.
If our team can reliably provide same-day setup and customer interviews show that speed matters, same-day setup may differentiate our service.
Every customer will choose the fastest provider.
Competitors cannot improve their setup time.
quizQuestions.answer: If our team can reliably provide same-day setup and customer interviews show that speed matters, same-day setup may differentiate our service.
quizQuestions.explanation: A defensible differentiation claim depends on evidence about both the venture’s capability and customer priorities; until those are tested, it should be framed as a hypothesis.

quizQuestions.question: A value proposition primarily answers the question:
options: How much does the product cost?
Why should a customer choose your product over alternatives?
When will the product launch?
How many employees does the company have?
quizQuestions.answer: Why should a customer choose your product over alternatives?
quizQuestions.explanation: A value proposition communicates the specific benefit you deliver and why it is the best option for your target customer.

quizQuestions.question: In Value Proposition Design, USP stands for:
options: Universal Service Plan
Unique Selling Point
User Support Portal
Unified Strategic Proposal
quizQuestions.answer: Unique Selling Point
quizQuestions.explanation: A Unique Selling Point (USP) is the specific feature or benefit that distinguishes a product from all competitors.

quizQuestions.question: Positioning in marketing refers to:
options: The physical location of your business
How a product is perceived in the minds of target customers relative to competitors
The position a CEO holds in a company
The placement of products on a store shelf
quizQuestions.answer: How a product is perceived in the minds of target customers relative to competitors
quizQuestions.explanation: Positioning shapes how customers think about your product — it is about the space your brand occupies in the customer's mind relative to alternatives.

quizQuestions.question: Which value proposition is most specific and customer-centered?
options: For busy high school students, our 15-minute planning tool turns assignments into a daily schedule so deadlines are easier to meet.
We make the best planning app for everyone.
Our company uses modern technology and has many features.
Students should choose us because our logo is memorable.
quizQuestions.answer: For busy high school students, our 15-minute planning tool turns assignments into a daily schedule so deadlines are easier to meet.
quizQuestions.explanation: A strong value proposition names the target customer, the problem or desired outcome, and a concrete benefit. Broad superiority claims, feature lists, and branding do not explain customer value.
